meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's easier to act your way into a new way of thinking than to think your way into a new way of acting'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Zig Ziglar. An anonymous chiastic aphorism, first documented in print in 1959 by psychologist O. Hobart Mowrer, who called it a saying he'd come upon.

answer.label: Not Zig Ziglar — an anonymous aphorism
answer.authorDates: Family of sayings documented from 1930; this exact wording by 1959 · no identifiable creator
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuinely anonymous aphorism. Quote Investigator traces it to an evolving family of chiastic sayings whose creators were unknown; this exact “new way of thinking / new way of acting” wording is first documented in 1959, when psychologist O. Hobart Mowrer introduced it as an aphorism he had merely “come upon.” Zig Ziglar used only a different feeling-variant and openly credited it to a friend — he did not originate this line.

source.heading: Where the wording is actually documented
source.excerpt: Recently the present writer came upon an aphorism to this effect: “It is easier to act your way into a new way of thinking than to think your way into a new way of acting.”
trail: 1930: the earliest documented ancestor appears at a Nebraska Sunday-School convention — “easier to act yourself into right thinking than to think yourself into right acting” — speaker unidentified, per Quote Investigator.
1959: the exact modern wording is first printed by psychologist O. Hobart Mowrer, who calls it an aphorism he “came upon” — no author is named.

1977: Zig Ziglar, in See You At the Top, quotes only a different variant — “you can’t ‘feel’ your way into a new way of acting, but you can ‘act’ your way into a new way of feeling” — and credits “my good friend Bruce Norman,” not himself.
Conclusion: QI finds “the creator (or creators) were anonymous” and that the phrasing evolved over decades.
source.excerptNote: O. Hobart Mowrer, in his comment in Critical Incidents in Psychotherapy (1959), p. 80 — the earliest print appearance of this exact wording, presented not as his own but as a saying he had “come upon.”
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous aphorism with no identifiable author; its earliest documented appearance (1959) postdates 1931 and is credited to no one. Because the origin of the wording is unknown, no public-domain status can be asserted, and there is no single rights-holder to name.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: An anonymous, evolving aphorism
author.metaLine: Documented from 1930; exact wording by 1959 · originator unknown
author.bio: This line is not one person’s coinage but a chiastic proverb that mutated over decades. Quote Investigator traces ancestors to a 1930 Sunday-school convention and finds the creators were anonymous. Missionary E. Stanley Jones popularized related versions in the 1930s–40s but did not invent them, and psychologist O. Hobart Mowrer printed this exact wording in 1959 as a saying he had simply “come upon.”

misattribution.heading: How Zig Ziglar got the credit
misattribution.intro: Ziglar is a top magnet for tidy, motivational chiasmus, and this line has the shape of something he’d say — so it drifted onto him. But the record shows the opposite of authorship.

items.why: In See You At the Top Ziglar quotes only a different feeling-variant — “you can’t ‘feel’ your way into a new way of acting, but you can ‘act’ your way into a new way of feeling” — and attributes it to “my good friend Bruce Norman,” per Quote Investigator. He never claimed the “thinking” line at all.
Jones spread related instances in his 1930s–40s books, and later writers (including Mowrer) sometimes credited him — but QI concludes he “did not really create them.”
The exact wording is widely re-quoted from Sternin’s work on positive deviance, one of many later hand-offs — not an origin, as the chronology shows.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: this is an anonymous aphorism whose exact form is first documented in 1959, presented even then as a saying already in circulation — not Zig Ziglar’s.

context.heading: Why the wording keeps shifting
lead: The saying is built on chiasmus — the mirrored “act your way into thinking / think your way into acting” structure — which makes it endlessly remixable. Over ninety years the verbs have swapped between act, live, and behave, and the nouns between right thinking, new way of thinking, and new way of feeling.

That plasticity is exactly why no single author can claim it: each speaker reshaped an already-circulating proverb. It survives in psychotherapy, recovery, and management literature precisely because it compresses a real idea — behavior can lead belief — into a memorable mirror.
context.pull: An idea old enough, and useful enough, to belong to everyone and no one.
